Cape May Live ·
· September 20, 2025 ·
I’ve spent the summers in Cape May my whole life, and I’ve grown up around people who are now feeling priced out of the very place they’ve always called home.
I get it—it’s not easy.
Back then, the houses here weren’t worth much, the town felt quieter, and your local bar was just a place where neighbors gathered without much fuss.
When it was mostly just Cape May people, there were a lot of vacant homes around town.
Now, many of those same houses are being fixed up and brought back to life.
That’s one of the biggest changes—what used to sit empty is now desirable, valuable, and alive again.
Cape May is the oldest seaside resort town in America, and every now and then it just needs a freshening up—whether locals like it or not.
If we don’t change, we will die.
That’s the hard truth of any town that wants to survive.
These days, Cape May has become incredibly desirable, and with that comes rising prices, tourists everywhere, and the shift from old parking meters to ParkMobile.
It all adds to the feeling that the town isn’t just “ours” anymore.
It’s a hard adjustment, and I understand why so many locals are frustrated.
At the same time, it’s worth remembering that without the influx of money and attention, Cape May might not have come back to life the way it has.
Businesses are thriving, the streets feel alive again, and the town is getting some of the care it desperately needed.
There are still problems, sure, but at least there’s hope they’ll get addressed.
And for those of us who stick it out, we still have our local summer after Labor Day—the fishing, the beach, and the peace of having it all without the crowds.
That’s when Cape May feels most like home.
It’s complicated—because while we do benefit from all this growth, we also feel the loss of the Cape May we grew up with.
